title: Love your enemies (Matthew 5:43–48)
hookLine: pray for those who persecute you; the sun rises on the evil and the good

cards: Tomorrow morning the sun will come up over your street. It will come through the window of the kindest person you know.

And it will come through the window of the person you like least in the world, at exactly the same time, just as warm. The rain will fall on both your yards. The sky doesn't check anyone's record first.
Jesus points to that ordinary fact, and builds a hard command on it.

teach.h: LOVE THY NEIGHBOR, HATE THINE ENEMY?
teach.b: Ye have heard, he says, love thy neighbor, and hate thine enemy. The first half is from Leviticus: love thy neighbor as thyself.
The second half isn't a verse anywhere in the Hebrew Bible, and nobody knows for sure where the saying came from.
The book of Proverbs, in fact, says: "If thine enemy be hungry, give him bread to eat; and if he be thirsty, give him water to drink."
Then, in the King James Bible: "But I say unto you, Love your enemies, bless them that curse you, do good to them that hate you, and pray for them which despitefully use you, and persecute you."
The word for love is agape, which Christian teachers often explain not as a warm feeling but as a choice to seek someone's good. You may never like your enemy. You can still want good for them.
"That ye may be the children of your Father which is in heaven: for he maketh his sun to rise on the evil and on the good, and sendeth rain on the just and on the unjust."
That's God's way, Jesus says: generous to everyone. If you love only those who love you, what reward is that? Even the tax collectors do the same.
Then the chapter's last line: be ye therefore perfect, even as your Father which is in heaven is perfect.
The Greek word, teleios, means whole, complete, grown up. Not flawless.
Complete in love, the way the sun is complete, shining on every yard. Christians have tried to live this in extreme places: forgiving the people who killed their families, praying for their jailers.
Jesus himself, Luke says, prayed from the cross for those crucifying him.

how: Some churches include prayers for enemies and those who wish harm in their regular intercessions, and Christians turn to this passage when facing conflict, war or personal injury.

games.q: someone has been cursing you and working against you. what does Jesus say to do?
o: bless them, do them good and pray for them.
games.why: "Love your enemies, bless them that curse you, do good to them that hate you." because God sends sun and rain on everyone.

practice: Let one person come to mind, someone who has hurt you, opposed you, or simply wears you out, and say their name quietly.

If you pray, pray for them: their health, their family, their peace; if you don't, simply wish them one good thing, sincerely. You don't have to feel warm or trust them; just picture the sun rising on their house, too.

wordCard.voice: Agape, love as a choice to seek someone's good, even an enemy's. The way the sun shines on everyone, evil and good alike.

orig.note: Greek: love, as a command to many. from agape: choosing another's good.

carryVoice: Your line: the sun shines on all. On their yard as well as yours. Until tomorrow.
